# Mahabhuta Nata to Ping An Hsing: The Same Five Forms, Renamed Down Fifteen Centuries

A karate student in any strip-mall dojo today learns a set of five training patterns called the Pinan. White belt, second form by green, the whole set done before black. The student is told these were composed around 1905 by a schoolteacher named Itosu, on Okinawa, to make karate teachable to children. Dukes tells a different story about that same word. Pinan, he says, is the Okinawan pronunciation of *Ping An* — "Peaceful Equanimity" — and Ping An is the Tang-dynasty Chinese name for a sequence of five moving meditations that began in India as the *Mahabhuta Nata*, the Five Great Elements forms.[^1] On this telling the children's exercise set is the tail end of a fifteen-hundred-year chain: five element-meditations, renamed in early Chinese as Wu Tai Hsing, renamed again in the Tang as Ping An, reverse-translated by later monks back into Sanskrit as Samashanti — and finally, in the late 1800s, taught to a man named Itosu by an esoteric Chinese monk. The forms a child does to learn balance, Dukes is claiming, were built to walk an adult through the five layers of their own consciousness.

## What This Actually Is

Strip the lineage claim away for a moment and look at the bottom layer. The *Mahabhuta Nata* — "Five Great Elements Nata" — is a set of moving forms, each form divided into five stages called *pratima*, with each stage assigned to one of the five elements: earth, water, fire, air, ether.[^1] A *nata* in Dukes's vocabulary is a kinetic practice, movement done as meditation; a *pratima* is one of its formal sequenced sections. So the structure is a frame inside a frame: five forms, each containing five element-stages. You do the earth section, then water, then fire, air, ether — and each section is meant to call up and expose the band of human nature that element governs, "be they psychological or physical."[^2] The form is a diagnostic walk through the self, element by element, where the discord in your movement reveals the discord in your mind.

The naming history is the spine of the page, so keep it straight. In early Buddhist Chinese the set was *Wu Tai Hsing* (Japanese: Godaigyo), "the five great elemental forms."[^3] Around the fourth and fifth centuries a second name appears — *Ping Hsing* (Byogyo), "the leveling or balancing elements" — and the particle *Ping* is doing heavy lifting, because *Ping* is also the oldest Chinese title for Ping Wang, the legendary founder of the Indian Ksatreya (warrior) caste, and probably a literal equivalent for the Sanskrit *Prasada*.[^3] In the Tang dynasty the set was renamed once more: the *Ping An (Peaceful Equanimity) Hsing*.[^4] Then later monks "reverse translated" Ping An back into Sanskrit as *Samashanti*, "non-differentiating peace" — a name Dukes calls not inappropriate.[^4]

The point of the *Ping/Sama* equivalence is not antiquarian. From the Tang onward, Dukes says, Buddhist terminology used *Ping* to stand for the Sanskrit *Sama* (together with, unified, conjoined) or *Samata* (characterized by joining or unification) — both words for a condition of calming, of blending into tranquil or equanimous mind.[^5] So the name of the form is the goal of the form. Ping An / Samashanti is not a label stuck on the outside; it is a one-word description of the state the five-stage walk is supposed to produce — unification, the very opposite of the scattered, confused consciousness most people live inside.[^5]

## The Mechanism: A Name That Records What the Practice Does

Here is the move that makes this more than a philology footnote. Most martial forms are named after a person, an animal, a place, or a count — Sanchin, the crane, Naihanchi, the second form. The Mahabhuta Nata's chain of names is different. Every renaming preserves the *function*, not the brand. Wu Tai Hsing names the material (five elemental forms). Ping Hsing names the action (leveling, balancing). Ping An names the result (peaceful equanimity). Samashanti names it again, translated, as "non-differentiating peace." Across four languages and fifteen centuries the thing being pointed at never changes: a sequence engineered to take a divided consciousness and bring it into balance, element by element.

Watch what the elements are doing inside the form. Earth is the body, water the emotions, fire the patterns of action, air the thoughts, ether the self-centeredness at the core.[^6] You cannot fake your way through the sequence. As Dukes puts it elsewhere, the intellectual facade is quickly penetrated by the demands of a kinetic presentation — you may convince yourself your mind is clear, but the rhythm and harmony of your movement will reveal the opposite.[^7] So the five-stage walk is a lie detector for the self. The water section drags up your emotional discord; the air section exposes your mental clutter; the ether section confronts the centeredness that organizes all the rest. Balance in the form *is* balance in the layer. That is why the result-name fits: when the five elements move in harmony, the consciousness running them is, by definition, *Ping An*.

And here is the discipline that guards it. The early masters laid down that each of the five *pratima* be studied for at least three years before the next — fifteen years, minimum, to begin to understand the whole sequence correctly, an emphasis Dukes says is still maintained in modern Chuan Fa.[^8] Only someone committed to something far greater than fame could persevere.[^8] Read that against the strip-mall dojo doing all five Pinan before black belt. The three-years-per-form rule is the difference between using the forms as a consciousness-diagnostic and collecting them as physical techniques. One layer of the self per three years is not slow teaching; it is the actual rate at which an element-band of a human being can be walked into balance.

## Synergies: What This Gives the Rest of the Vault

This page is the connective tissue for half the Dukes corpus. [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/nata-kinetic-practice-movement-meditation|Nata: Kinetic Practice as Movement Meditation]] defines the category; the Mahabhuta Nata is its flagship instance — the specific nata that organizes the whole element-by-element pedagogy. [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/five-elements-consciousness-manifestations-detailed|Five Elements as Consciousness Manifestations]] supplies the content of each of the five stages; this page supplies the *vehicle* that walks a practitioner through them in sequence. Without the Mahabhuta Nata, the five-element scheme is a chart on a wall. With it, the chart becomes a fifteen-year moving curriculum.

It also gives [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/prasada-consciousness-based-energy|Prasada: Consciousness-Based Energy]] an unexpected etymological handshake — Dukes derives the *Ping* particle partly from *Prasada* (via *Rupaprasada*), tying the elemental-form name back into the healing vocabulary, and noting that the Wu Tai Hsing functioned as auto-physiotherapeutic healing as much as meditation.[^3] The forms heal and the forms reveal; the name carries both. And for [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/sthana-rigid-mental-stance|Sthana: The Rigid Mental Stance]] this page supplies the arena. Dukes says the hsing is a situational encounter where the opponent is one's own sthana — the form is a solitary battle against your own rigid self-position, and its victory is the realization of that position's nature.[^9] The Mahabhuta Nata is where sthana gets fought.

For the contested history below, this page is also the vault's anchor for one of the corpus's load-bearing quarantine flags — the Itosu/Li Tsun San claim — which connects it directly to the [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/bodhidharma-revisionist-biography|Bodhidharma Revisionist Biography]] page, where the same pattern (a privately-warranted lineage running against the standard scholarly account) is the central problem.

## Analytical Case Study: One Sentence That Rewrites Karate History

The detonating sentence is buried mid-paragraph and stated as plain fact: "A much later Ryukuan student of Chuan Fa named Itosu (Chinese: Su Chow) mentions studying a set of Ping An Hsing under the Chinese esoteric monk Li Tsun San (Japanese: Rijunsan) in the late 1800's."[^4] Read it cold and it is a small biographical note. Read it against what every karate history book says and it is a grenade.

The standard account is not vague. Anko Itosu (1831–1915) is credited with *composing* the Pinan kata himself, around 1901–1907, as a graded curriculum for introducing karate into Okinawan public schools. He is the author, not the inheritor. Dukes's sentence quietly removes the authorship. In his telling Itosu did not invent five forms; he *received* a set of Ping An Hsing — already named, already ancient, already the Tang-renamed Mahabhuta Nata — from a named esoteric Chinese monk. The Pinan, on this reading, are not a turn-of-the-century teaching aid. They are the visible Okinawan terminus of a Buddhist consciousness-practice that runs back through Tang China to India.

This is exactly the kind of claim that has to be quarantined rather than swallowed, and exactly the kind that is load-bearing if you don't. If Dukes is right, the children's exercise set carries an esoteric pedigree and a fifteen-year diagnostic intent that modern karate has completely forgotten. If the standard account is right, Itosu composed the forms and Dukes (or his tradition) has retrofitted a lineage onto them. The vault cannot adjudicate this — it can only hold the two accounts in tension and refuse to let the more romantic one harden into fact. [CONTESTED] The honest reading is that the *etymological* spine (Pinan ← Ping An ← Wu Tai Hsing ← Mahabhuta Nata; Ping = Sama) is genuinely interesting and partly checkable, while the *transmission* claim (Itosu learned, did not compose) contradicts the documentary record and rests on Dukes's own lineage warrant. Keep both visible.

## Implementation Workflow

Third year. You have done nothing but the earth *pratima* — the first of the five — for thirty-six months, and tonight the teacher finally says the word for the second one: water.

Before you are allowed to start it, he makes you do the earth section one more time, alone, in the center of the floor. You drop your weight. The form is in your legs now, not your head; you stopped thinking about it sometime in the second year. Heel, hip, the long settle into the stance — earth, the body, the ground of the whole sequence. It is solid. It is, finally, *Ping* in that one layer: level, balanced, quiet. Three years bought you one element's worth of equanimity.

Then water. And the floor drops out. The second *pratima* asks the body to flow where the first asked it to root, and everything you stabilized comes loose at the emotional layer — the form turns choppy, the breath snatches, a flush of frustration you did not know was in there rises straight off the movement and into your face. You feel, in your own clumsiness, exactly the thing the water element governs. The intellectual facade is gone; the kinetic presentation has read you out loud.[^7] And you understand, standing there sweating, why the masters said three years. Not because the water form is physically hard. Because the band of yourself it exposes takes that long to walk into balance — and there are three more elements waiting behind it, each its own season of being found out. Fifteen years is not the time to learn five dances. It is the time to be shown five layers of yourself, one at a time, by your own moving body.

## The Lineage-as-Technique Failure (Diagnostic Signs)

- You collect forms. You know more kata than your seniors and you experience this as progress — when Dukes's whole warning is that "one who knows more is one who knows more," and nothing else.[^10]
- You can perform all five Pinan but could not say which layer of consciousness any one of them is meant to expose. The diagnostic intent has evaporated and only the choreography remains.
- Your dojo runs students through the full set in two or three years to a black belt. The three-years-per-element floor has been read as a quaint old ceiling and discarded; the forms now teach balance the way a worksheet teaches arithmetic.
- You treat the name as decoration. "Pinan" or "Peaceful Mind" is a label on a certificate, not a description of a state you are actually being walked toward — the result-name has been severed from the result.
- You chase the competition gradient instead: exchanging the old self of a contender for the new Self of a champion, fighting on until too injured or too old, which Dukes names as the same self-misunderstanding the forms were built to dissolve.[^11]
- You feel the elemental discord in your movement — the choppiness, the absent rhythm — and you treat it as a fitness problem to be drilled away, rather than as the form telling you the truth about the layer of yourself it just touched.[^7]

## Evidence, Tensions, Open Questions

The strongest part of this material is the part nobody needs to take on faith: the *internal* logic of the naming. That *Ping* maps to *Sama/Samata*, that Ping An reverse-translates plausibly to Samashanti, that "Peaceful Equanimity" names a unification-state rather than a person or animal — this is coherent and partly checkable against Buddhist technical vocabulary. [PLAUSIBLE — needs corroboration] The weakest part is the transmission claim. Itosu learning the Pinan from Li Tsun San directly contradicts the standard karate-historical consensus that Itosu *composed* the Pinan kata around 1901–1907 as a school curriculum. Dukes states the learned-not-composed version as settled fact, cites it to his own reference notes, and does not engage the composition account at all. This is a load-bearing quarantine: it cannot be resolved here and must not be silently adopted. [CONTESTED]

A second tension sits inside Dukes's own frame. He says the *Mahabhuta Nata* predates the Taoist "five elements / five forms / five activities fist" boxing traditions that are "often claimed to be the originals" of pentamerous self-defense sequences.[^12] That is a priority claim — Buddhist element-forms first, Taoist element-boxing later — made against a Chinese martial tradition that asserts the reverse. The vault preserves it as Dukes's position, not as adjudicated history.

Open questions. First: is the *Pancadravya/Pancatattva* naming dispute — the Vaibhasika sect calling the forms "Five Natures" (dravya) versus the "Five Essences" (tattva) reading — a real sectarian record or a doctrinal point projected onto the form-names? Dukes reports that Vasubandhu argued repeatedly against the Vaibhasika *dravya* usage, saying it implied permanence in what is intrinsically impermanent.[^13] If that argument is historical, the very *name* of the form set was a battleground in the impermanence debate. Second: if the etymology holds but the transmission doesn't, what *is* the relationship between the genuinely ancient Chinese Ping An material and Itosu's Pinan — independent invention that happens to share a name, partial inheritance dressed as composition, or composition over a remembered older template? The page flags the fork; nothing here closes it.

## Author Tensions & Convergences

This page sits on top of one of the corpus's most exposed nerves, and the honest thing is to name where Dukes is standing when he makes the claim. He writes as Shifu Nagaboshi Tomio, abbot of Kongoryuji, and his decisive evidence for the Itosu transmission is a cluster of his own reference notes — the same privately-warranted apparatus that anchors the Bodhidharma material. So the Itosu/Li Tsun San sentence is not a neutral report; it is a lineage-internal memory presented in the register of established fact. Felt from inside the tradition, it is simply what was passed down. Read from outside, against the documentary record of Itosu composing the Pinan for Okinawan schools, it is a claim the tradition has every motive to hold and no independent corroboration to support. Both readings are true to their vantage, and the vault keeps both rather than picking the flattering one.

Against the vault's Samuel and White critical-historical corpus, the friction is the familiar one. Samuel and White would not necessarily quarrel with the *linguistic* observation — Buddhist terms did migrate and reverse-translate, and *Ping/Sama* is the kind of equivalence philology can test. What they would refuse is the leap from "this name has a Buddhist genealogy" to "therefore this specific Okinawan kata was transmitted, not composed." That is precisely the move — backfilling a clean ancient lineage onto a modern practice — that White's work on the invention of the seven-chakra system and Samuel's on the dating of Tantric yoga were written to catch. Where Dukes converges with them, almost despite himself, is in his contempt for the form-collector and the competition-champion: his unsentimental picture of the modern practitioner accumulating kata and trophies in self-misunderstanding[^10][^11] is closer to White's power-driven, fear-driven yogis than to any heroic martial-arts romance. He romanticizes the *lineage* and de-romanticizes the *practitioner* — a revealing split.

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

**[[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/voice-print-vast-framework|VAST Voice Print]] (business).** The VAST framework treats a creator's recognizable voice as a transmissible artifact — something that can be captured, named, and carried forward across instances without the originating person. The Mahabhuta Nata's naming chain is the same problem in a contemplative key, and it surfaces a hazard the business frame underplays. Across Wu Tai Hsing → Ping An → Samashanti → Pinan, what was *meant* to be transmitted was a function (a consciousness-balancing practice), but what reliably survives transmission is the *form* — the visible choreography — while the function silently drops out, leaving a strip-mall Pinan that looks identical and does nothing it was built to do. The insight neither domain reaches alone: a transmissible artifact degrades along a predictable axis — the externally visible layer (the moves, the cadence, the surface style) is robustly copyable, and the internal generating intent (which layer of consciousness this is supposed to expose, why this word and not that one) is the part that evaporates first. A "voice print" or a kata can be faithfully reproduced and still be hollow, because the part that made it load-bearing was never in the copyable surface. The three-years-per-element rule is, read this way, an anti-degradation protocol: it refuses to transmit the next form until the *function* of the current one has actually landed in the student. Most transmission systems — creative, martial, institutional — have no such gate, which is exactly why they decay into surface.

**[[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/strategic-use-of-legitimacy-and-pedigree|Strategic Use of Legitimacy and Pedigree]] (behavioral-mechanics).** A claimed lineage is a power move before it is a historical statement, and the Itosu/Li Tsun San sentence is a clean specimen. Attaching a modern practice to an ancient, esoteric, named transmission does specific work: it converts a teaching aid into a sacred inheritance, raises the cost of questioning it, and transfers the authority of the deep past onto the present holder of the line. Behavioral-mechanics names this as a deliberate tactic of legitimation. Dukes's page lets us see it operating sincerely from the *inside* — not as cynical manufacture but as a tradition's genuine self-understanding, which is what makes pedigree claims so hard to audit: the people making them are usually not lying, they are remembering. The combined insight, available from neither field alone: the most durable legitimacy claims are the ones the claimant fully believes, because sincerity removes every behavioral tell the skeptic would normally read. The critical historian's job and the propagandist's target are therefore the same object — a pedigree held in good faith — and the only available check is external documentation (here, the karate-historical record of composition), not the demeanor or honesty of the source. Which is precisely why Dukes's *etymology* can be partly trusted and his *transmission* cannot: one is checkable against the language, the other rests entirely on the sincerity of the line.

## The Live Edge

**Sharpest implication:** the part of any transmitted practice that survives is the part you can see, and the part you can see is rarely the part that mattered. A child's balance exercise and a fifteen-year consciousness-diagnostic can be the *identical* sequence of movements — which means the entire difference between them lives in something no recording, no diagram, and no lineage certificate can carry: the intent the form is performed with, and the rate at which it is taught.

**Generative questions:**
- If function reliably evaporates while form survives transmission, is there any transmission system that protects the function — and is the three-years-per-element gate (refuse to pass on the next layer until this one has landed) the general solution, or only the contemplative one?
- The naming chain records the *goal* (Ping An = the equanimity the practice produces). What would a martial or creative form named after its *failure mode* instead of its goal teach a student that a goal-name hides?
- If Itosu composed rather than inherited, is a sincerely-believed false lineage *functionally* different from a true one — does the practice work worse because the pedigree is retrofitted, or does belief in the lineage do its own real work regardless of the history?

## Connected Concepts

- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/nata-kinetic-practice-movement-meditation|Nata: Kinetic Practice as Movement Meditation]] — the category; the Mahabhuta Nata is its flagship element-by-element instance.
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/five-elements-consciousness-manifestations-detailed|Five Elements as Consciousness Manifestations]] — supplies the content of each of the five pratima stages.
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/prasada-consciousness-based-energy|Prasada: Consciousness-Based Energy]] — the Ping particle's etymological tie back into the healing vocabulary.
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/sthana-rigid-mental-stance|Sthana: The Rigid Mental Stance]] — the solitary opponent the hsing is fought against.
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/shipalohanshou-eighteen-arahant-hands|Shipalohanshou: The 18 Arahant Hands]] — the sibling nata/pratima lineage, transmitted by Bodhidharma at Shaolin.
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/bodhidharma-revisionist-biography|Bodhidharma Revisionist Biography]] — the same privately-warranted-lineage-vs-standard-account problem, on a different transmission.
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/hubs/bodhisattva-warriors-chuan-fa-hub|Bodhisattva Warriors: Chuan Fa Hub]] — territory map for the Dukes corpus.

# The Women Who Never Got Out of the House

## One Sentence, and It Inverts the Whole Episode

Everyone knows the rāsa. The flute at night, the women running out of their houses, the circle, the dance.

Almost nobody knows this, and it is in the same chapter:

> "**Some gopis were in the inner quarters and couldn't find a means of coming out.** Filled with love for Krishna, they closed their eyes and meditated on him. The torment of being separated from their beloved was fierce and impossible to withstand. It cleansed all that was inauspicious. **They obtained Achyuta in their meditation and the bliss of that embrace exhausted their auspicious deeds.** They united with the paramatman, their minds regarding him as a paramour. **They gave up their bodies, full of gunas, and were instantly freed of all bondage.**"[^1]

They never leave the room. They never see him. They die on the spot and are completely liberated.

And the volume states it in one clause, in passing, before the dance has even started — and never mentions them again.

## Now Look at the Ones Who Made It

Follow the women who got out.

Within the hour he vanishes on them (10.30). They wander the forest asking trees where he went. They find another woman's footprints beside his and work out, forensically, that he took someone else. They sing the Gopī-gīta and ask him whether what he is doing to them counts as murder (10.31).

He comes back. There is a dance. It ends, and he sends them home.

Then: still lamenting to a bee at 10(47). Still lamenting to Balarāma, who comes back when Kṛṣṇa does not, at 10(65). **Still lamenting at 10(82), decades later, at a solar eclipse, as middle-aged women.**

⚑ **The women who could not attend were free within the hour. The women who attended were still grieving sixty chapters later.** Both facts are the text's. It never puts them together.

The 10(82) scene is worth sitting on, because it is where the asymmetry stops being a matter of a few chapters. Kṛṣṇa is at Kurukṣetra for an eclipse. The gopīs are there. They are no longer girls. And the conversation is the same conversation — the same complaint, the same unhealed absence, delivered by women who have had entire lives happen to them in between.

Whatever the rāsa did for the women who attended it, **it did not close.** The volume tracks the wound for the length of a human life and never reports it healing.

Against that, four lines: closed eyes, an unbearable separation, and *"instantly freed."*

## The Merit Is Spent, Not Earned

Look again at the mechanism, because it is not the one you would expect:

> "the bliss of that embrace **exhausted their auspicious deeds**"

Not *rewarded*. **Exhausted.** The embrace consumed the stock.

That is a strange piece of accounting for a devotional text. The ordinary picture is accumulation — merit builds, and at some threshold it purchases an outcome. Here the outcome arrives and *burns the balance*, and the burning is what frees them, because what is left when the auspicious deeds are gone is a person with nothing outstanding in either direction.

Set beside the fried grain seven chapters earlier — a seed rendered infertile rather than removed — and this volume has now given two mechanisms in which **attainment works by disabling a stock rather than by adding to one**.

And there is a reason the accounting has to work this way, which the passage does not state but its own logic requires. *Auspicious deeds* are a claim on future outcomes. They buy births, conditions, destinations. A person still holding a balance is a person with results still owed to them — which is another way of saying a person with more life scheduled.

So the merit is not incidental to the bondage. **It is a form of it.** Burning it is not the price of liberation; it is the same event described from the other side. What the embrace destroys is the reason there would have to be a next thing.

⚠ Held at the register the evidence carries. The passage gives the sequence — embrace, exhausted deeds, body given up, *"instantly freed of all bondage"* — and does not supply the reasoning above. `[n=1 OBSERVED]`, and the interpretation is offered as a reading of why the clause is ordered as it is, **not as the volume's stated position.**

## What They Did Not Have

Worth being precise about what the confined women lacked, because the list is total.

No sight of him. No touch. No dance. No conversation. No journey — they did not even get to run. And no *permission*: they were shut in, and the text says plainly they *"couldn't find a means of coming out."*

What they had was one thing: *"the torment of being separated from their beloved was fierce and impossible to withstand."*

⚑ **The volume's most complete liberation in the Tenth Skandha is granted on the strength of an unrelieved absence.** Not a practice, not a vision, not an encounter. The pain of not getting there is the entire operative content.

## The Doctrine He Gives Later Is Weaker Than This

Kṛṣṇa produces something like this claim himself, much later, and it does not go as far.

At 10(47), through Uddhava, he explains the separation as engineered — *"I, your beloved, am now far distant from your sight. This is with the objective of attracting your minds towards me."* And he adds a clause covering those who never got to the rāsa at all: because they thought about his valour, *"they will obtain me."*

Compare the two. His version: absence is instrumental, and the excluded will *eventually* obtain him. The narrator's version at 10(29): the excluded **already did**, instantly, and more completely than anyone present.

**The protagonist's own doctrine is a weaker restatement of something the narrator had already asserted eighteen chapters earlier**, and neither passage acknowledges the other.

## Implementation Workflow

You do not get into the room. The meeting happens, the decision is made, and you were not there — and eighteen months later you notice the people who were in that room are still relitigating it, and you are not, because you never had a version of it to defend.

You wanted a thing badly and were refused outright. Cleanly, early, with no ambiguity. Compare yourself to the person who got it for two months and then lost it. Which of you is still checking?

You are prevented from going to the funeral. You sit in a room a thousand miles away at the hour it happens, and the grief has nothing to attach to and nowhere to go, and something in it finishes that does not finish for the people who stood at the grave and had a day to get through.

None of these is a recommendation. The volume is not recommending it either. It is reporting an asymmetry and moving on.

## Analytical Case Study: Why This Fold Was Refused

This page exists because a compression check reversed an earlier decision, and the reversal is instructive about the material.

The merge pass treated the confined gopīs as a detail inside the rāsa — one clause in a chapter about a dance. That is how the text presents it, and it is how nearly every reading treats it.

The compression check refused the fold on three grounds. **Its own mechanism:** liberation without attendance, with merit spent rather than accrued, which the rāsa page does not contain. **Its own worked example:** the confined women, whose outcome is stated and complete. **Its own cross-domain pull**, which the rāsa page has none of.

⚑ **And the deciding consideration was that folding it would have reproduced the text's own error.** The Purāṇa buries its sharpest claim about access in a subordinate clause and never returns to it. A vault page that made it a subsection of the dance would have performed the same burial with better formatting.

## What the Volume Does Not Do With It

No character notices. Parīkṣit, who interrupts twice in these five chapters to raise moral objections, does not ask about it. Śuka does not flag it. It is not cited in the Eleventh Skandha's long argument about who may approach, where it would be the strongest available evidence.

⚠ And that has to be stated carefully. **This is a claim about the range read** — 10(12) through 12(13). It is not a claim about Volumes 1–2, and no page here asserts the corpus never returns to it.

What can be said is that within this volume, the one passage that shows total liberation granted to people who did nothing, went nowhere and saw nothing is left exactly where it was dropped.

## Evidence, Tensions, Open Questions

**The strongest support** is that the passage is not ambiguous. It does not say the confined women were consoled, or that they attained something lesser, or that they were rewarded later. It says they obtained him, their merit was exhausted, they gave up their bodies, and they were *"instantly freed of all bondage."* Every term is the vocabulary of final liberation.

**The tension, preserved.** The volume's whole rāsa apparatus — the lecture, the rebuttal, the circle, the multiplication, the non-imitation clause at 10(33) — is built to justify an episode that this clause makes soteriologically unnecessary. **If absence works better, the dance is not the mechanism, and the volume never addresses the gap.**

**A second tension.** The attending gopīs are the volume's exemplars of supreme devotion, and they are also, on the text's own timeline, the ones it leaves grieving for decades. Both are the volume's positions. **Do not average them into a story where the lamentation is itself the reward** — that reading is available, it is the tradition's, and 10(29) does not make it: the confined women get the *"instantly freed"* language and the attending women never do.

**Open question.** *"Exhausted their auspicious deeds"* is the mechanism. Does the volume use it elsewhere? The fried grain at 10(22) is adjacent but not identical — a stock rendered inert rather than consumed. `[n=2 SUGGESTIVE]` on attainment-by-disabling-a-stock, and the two mechanisms should not be merged on that evidence.

## Author Tensions & Convergences

Against [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/the-gopis-as-supreme-bhaktas|The Gopīs as Supreme Bhaktas]], this page is the internal complication that material does not carry. The gopīs' supremacy is normally grounded in the intensity of what they had — the encounter, the *rasa*, the completeness of the relationship. 10(29) grades a group *above* them on the strength of not having had it.

That does not overturn the standard reading. It does mean the vault should hold that the volume's own text supplies a higher outcome to a group it mentions once and forgets.

Set against [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/the-lecture-before-the-dance|He Argued Against It First]], the two passages sit in the same chapter and pull opposite ways. The lecture-and-rebuttal sequence is the volume working hard to establish that these women were *right to come*. Fifteen lines earlier, it has already said the ones who could not come did better. **The chapter argues for the journey and reports that the journey was not required.**

Against [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/fried-grain-cannot-sprout|The Seed That Stays a Seed]], the pairing is mechanical rather than thematic and it is the more useful one. Both are stock-disabling mechanisms; one renders a stock inert and leaves it, the other consumes a stock entirely. **Neither is the accumulation model the tradition's practice literature runs on**, and both are stated in the Tenth Skandha within seven chapters of each other.

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

**[[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/near-miss-effect|Near-Miss Effect]]** — Wadhwa's finding: on scratch cards, people who *almost* won subsequently spend more than people who actually won and more than people who clearly lost. The near-win produces elevated arousal and sustained pursuit that neither outcome at the ends of the distribution produces.

The rāsa splits its women into exactly those three conditions, and the volume tracks all three across sixty chapters.

**Clear loss** — the confined gopīs. Never got out, never saw him. Resolved instantly and permanently. **Actual win** — nobody, quite, but the woman he takes aside at 10(30) is closest, and she is abandoned within the hour and humiliated. **Near miss** — everyone who attended: they got the dance and lost him, and they are still pursuing at 10(47), 10(65) and 10(82).

⚑ **What neither field gives alone: the volume reads the near-miss profile as spiritual attainment, and the psychology reads it as a motivational artefact of the reward schedule — and the two descriptions fit the same women equally well.** Decades of undiminished longing is what the devotional tradition means by *viraha* and what Wadhwa's data would predict from a partial reinforcement. This is not a debunking; the mechanism does not decide the meaning. But it does yield a genuinely uncomfortable question the tradition does not ask: **the gopīs' celebrated inexhaustible longing may be a property of how the encounter was terminated rather than of how much they loved him** — and the volume's own control group, the women who were cleanly excluded, is the evidence, because they stopped.

**[[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/hedonic-reversal-dopamine-receptor-upregulation|Hedonic Reversal and Dopamine Receptor Upregulation]]** — Koe's claim that taking intense pleasures away raises the floor of sensitivity until ordinary things become vivid again. The treadmill run backwards: deprivation as the route to intensity.

The confined gopīs are that mechanism at its terminal setting. Total deprivation, no relief available, and the text is explicit that the deprivation itself is the operative agent — *"the torment of being separated… was fierce and impossible to withstand. **It cleansed all that was inauspicious.**"* The torment does the cleansing. Not the meditation, not the love: the unbearability.

⚑ **The insight: hedonic reversal is described as a cycle, and this is the case where it does not cycle.** Koe's version restores sensitivity so the ordinary can be enjoyed again — deprivation is a phase, and the payoff is a return. Here there is no return. The sensitivity rises past the point where a body can hold it and the body is given up. **That names the boundary condition the wellness framing does not model: the same curve, extended, does not produce a richer life but exits it.** And it identifies what makes the mechanism safe in Koe's version — not the deprivation's depth but the *availability of relief*, which is precisely the variable the confined women did not have.

## The Live Edge

**Sharpest implication.** **The most complete liberation in the Tenth Skandha is granted to women who were locked in a room, and the text spends one clause on it before returning to the dance it was not required for.** Their merit was not rewarded — it was spent — and what freed them was the pain of not arriving.

**Generative questions.**
- If the excluded did better, what was the rāsa for? The volume defends the episode twice and never asks whether it was necessary.
- The attending gopīs' longing is the tradition's model of devotion, and it fits a partial-reinforcement profile exactly. Does anything distinguish inexhaustible love from an unclosed loop, and would this text accept the question?
- Merit is *exhausted* by the embrace. What kind of economy is this, in which arriving spends the balance rather than earning against it?

## Connected Concepts

- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/the-gopis-as-supreme-bhaktas|The Gopīs as Supreme Bhaktas]] — the standard grounding of their supremacy, and the group this chapter grades above them

The attending gopīs' subsequent lamentation is at 10(30), 10(31), 10(47), 10(65) and 10(82); Kṛṣṇa's weaker restatement of the absence doctrine is at 10(47). ⚠ **Debroy's note 192 covers this chapter and the four that follow:** *"There are various interpretations of Krishna's use of yoga maya. There are also extensive commentaries on these five chapters. **We have deliberately kept the translation simple.**"* The *yoga-māyā* and liberation vocabulary in this passage is exactly where a commentarial tradition would read otherwise, and this translation declines to.

# The Person I Want to Forget Is Lying in My Heart

## The Decision That Summons the Thing

You decide to stop thinking about someone.

Not vaguely — you actually decide it, with a reason, having worked out that the thinking is costing you more than it returns. It is a good decision. You may even feel the small relief that comes with having settled something.

**And then they are there.**

Not gradually. Not later that evening. **At the moment of deciding**, more vividly than they have been all week — because the decision required you to specify what you were giving up, and specifying it put it in front of you.

Antya-līlā 17 records that sequence, in Rādhā's voice, in four hundred-year-old Bengali, with the mechanism stated precisely enough that it would pass as a description of the experiment that named it.[^1]

## The Reasoning and Its Result

She reasons her way to peace, and the reasoning is sound.

*"**If I give up hope of meeting Kṛṣṇa, I shall then be happy. Therefore, let us stop this most inglorious discussion of Kṛṣṇa.**"*[^2]

That is a correct analysis. The hope is what hurts; abandoning the hope removes the source; the practical step is to stop the discussion that keeps it alive. **Anybody who has ever talked themselves out of something has produced that paragraph.**

And the instant she resolves it:

*"**The person I want to forget is lying in My heart.**"*[^3]

**The resolution is the summoning.** Not a failure of the resolution, not a relapse after it — the two are one event, and the corpus reports them in that order with nothing between.

Then she reclassifies him, which is the part that shows how completely the move has failed:

*"This Cupid, who has conquered the whole world and entered My heart, **is My greatest enemy, for He does not allow Me to forget Him.**"*[^4]

## What the Sentence Gets Exactly Right

Take the two clauses of the reclassification separately, because they are doing different work.

**"Who has conquered the whole world and entered My heart."** The agency is his. She is not describing her own attachment; she is describing an incursion.

**"For He does not allow Me to forget Him."** And the grievance is specifically about **the failure of forgetting** — not about absence, not about betrayal, not about longing. The thing she is aggrieved by is that a mental operation she attempted did not work.

That is an unusually precise complaint. **She is not saying she misses him. She is saying she cannot execute the instruction she gave herself**, and she has correctly identified that as a separate problem from the missing.

**And she attributes the failure to him.** Which is where a modern account would part company — the failure is a property of the operation, not of the person being forgotten — and it is also, on the corpus's own theology, not obviously wrong, because the being in question is held to actually be present in the heart.[^5]

**The passage is therefore simultaneously an accurate phenomenological report and a theological claim**, and its accuracy is what makes the theological claim persuasive from inside.

## Analytical Case Study: Why It Has to Fail

The mechanism deserves stating in full because the passage states half of it and the half it omits is the load-bearing half.

**To suppress a thought, you must first specify the thought.** *Stop thinking about Kṛṣṇa* is an instruction that contains its own object. There is no way to issue it without holding the thing in mind, because the instruction has to be *about* something in order to be an instruction at all.

**And then you must monitor.** How do you know whether the suppression is working? By checking whether the thought is present. **The check is a retrieval.** Every audit of your own success at not-thinking is an instance of the thinking.

So the operation has two components and both produce the forbidden content. **Suppression is not an attempt that sometimes fails; it is a procedure that generates its own object twice over**, once in the specification and repeatedly in the monitoring.

Which is why the corpus's ordering is exactly right. **The appearance follows the resolution immediately** — not after a delay, not under stress, but at the moment the decision is formed, because forming the decision is one of the two generating operations.

**Rādhā does not fail to forget. She performs, correctly and completely, an operation whose correct and complete performance is remembering.**

And there is a third component that the passage supplies and the mechanism's usual statement does not: **she announced it to somebody.**

*Let us stop this most inglorious discussion* is addressed to companions. The resolution is not private; it is a proposal, made aloud, that a group cease a topic — which means the specification has now been produced once by her and installed in several other people, each of whom will thereafter be monitoring the same prohibition.

**A publicly declared suppression is a suppression with additional monitors.** Every person who heard the instruction now has a reason to notice the topic, and their noticing will surface it — in a glance, in an avoidance, in the visible effort of not mentioning it.

Which is worth naming because the public version is the common one. **Almost nobody resolves to stop thinking about something silently**; they tell a friend, they announce it, they make it accountable — and accountability is monitoring, distributed.

## The Corpus Reads It as Divinity

Now the part that matters for reading this text, and it is where the page has to be careful.

**The corpus offers this as evidence of Kṛṣṇa's nature.** He is irresistible; he has conquered the world; he is present in the heart and cannot be evicted. The impossibility of forgetting is a fact about him.

That is not an unreasonable inference from the data available in 1615. **The observation is real, the sequence is real, and the explanation on offer accounts for it.** What the tradition lacked was any comparison case — because the passage is about one being, and there is no control condition in which somebody tries to forget something ordinary and finds it equally impossible.

**The comparison case is what a laboratory supplies**, and it comes out the same for a white bear.[^6]

**Which does not settle the theology and does settle the mechanism.** If the sequence occurs identically for a trivial object, then the sequence is not evidence about the object — and the corpus's inference, though honest, rests on the one variable it could not vary.

That is worth stating plainly rather than triumphantly. **A four-hundred-year-old text arrived at a genuine cognitive finding, described it accurately, and attributed it to the wrong variable for want of a comparison it had no way to run.** The description survives; the attribution does not.

## What Follows for Anybody Actually Trying

The practical upshot is not *stop trying to forget*, which is not advice.

**The operations that work are the ones that do not name the object.** Attention placed elsewhere is not suppression — it does not require specifying what is being avoided and it involves no monitoring, which is why distraction outperforms resolve and why nobody feels good about that.

**And the second thing that works is dropping the audit.** Much of the pain in Rādhā's position is not the presence of the thought but the discovery, repeatedly, that the thought is present — and that discovery is manufactured entirely by checking. **A person who stops grading their own forgetting loses most of the suffering and none of the ground.**

The corpus does not supply either of these and it is worth being clear why. **In this tradition the failure is the desired outcome.** Rādhā is not supposed to succeed; her inability to forget is the highest condition available in the entire system, and the passage is placed among the exalted material rather than among the discipline cases.[^7]

**Which is the strangest thing about it.** The corpus has described the ironic-process mechanism with complete accuracy and has no interest in defeating it, because it has found the one context in which failing to stop thinking about something is not a problem to be solved.

## The Layers

Layer A supplies the reasoning, the resolution, the immediate appearance and the reclassification as enemy.[^8]

Layer B expands the passage into the *mahābhāva* of separation and Rādhā's supreme position among the devotees.[^9]

Worth marking the difference in what each finds notable. **Layer A's interest is sequential** — she decided, and then he was there — and the passage's force is entirely in the ordering.

**Layer B's interest is positional.** It is concerned with what the episode establishes about Rādhā's rank, and the sequence is the occasion rather than the content.

**The mechanism is only visible in the ordering**, and a reader arriving through the commentary meets a doctrine about supreme love rather than a description of what happens when a person decides to stop.

## Implementation Workflow

You have decided to stop thinking about something. **Expect it immediately and do not read the arrival as a relapse.** The decision is one of the two operations that produce the thought, so the appearance is the decision working exactly as specified — and treating it as a failure adds a second decision, which produces it again.

You are checking whether you have succeeded at not-thinking. **Stop checking.** The audit is a retrieval, and most of what hurts in this situation is not the presence of the thought but the repeated discovery of its presence, which is manufactured entirely by looking.

You want the thing to actually recede. **Use operations that do not name it.** Attention placed on something else is not suppression: it specifies nothing and monitors nothing. That is why distraction outperforms resolve, and it is worth accepting even though it feels like the less serious method.

You have found a mechanism in a single compelling case. **Assume the object was not the variable until you have a boring one.** This passage is the standing example — an accurate description, an honest inference, and the wrong attribution, for want of a comparison nobody in 1615 could have run.

Somebody tells you they cannot stop thinking about someone. **Do not treat it as weakness, and do not supply the instruction.** *Try to stop* is the operation that generates the content, and it is the first thing everybody says.

## Evidence, Tensions, Open Questions

The evidence is a short first-person passage with a stated resolution, an immediate contrary result, and an explicit reclassification naming the failure of forgetting as the grievance.[^10]

**The tension the source doesn't close: the passage is offered as evidence about Kṛṣṇa and the same sequence occurs for any object.** The corpus had no comparison case and could not have had one, and the inference is honest and unsupported.

**A second one.** The corpus describes the mechanism with precision and has no interest in the remedy, because in this tradition the mechanism's output is the goal. **Every other tradition that noticed this treated it as a problem.**

**Open:** whether this passage is Rādhā's, Caitanya's, or the author's. It is delivered by a man in the *gopīs'* mood, recorded by a secretary, memorised, and composed eighty years later.[^11] **Four candidate authors for one of the most psychologically accurate sentences in the corpus**, and no way to distribute the credit.

## Author Tensions & Convergences

This page and [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/madana-and-mohana|Mādana and Mohana]] are the instance and its classification. **That page holds *citra-jalpa*, the varieties of mad talk, and the claim that in separation one experiences manifestation; this is the cleanest single case of manifestation-in-absence in the corpus** — and it arrives through an ordinary cognitive route the taxonomy does not mention.

Against [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/condemning-providence|Condemning Providence]] it is the same speaker in the same condition taking the opposite tack. **There the response to unbearable separation is sustained accusation — of the system, then of the beloved, then of herself; here it is a reasoned decision to stop** — and both fail, and the corpus records both as exalted.

And it belongs beside [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/krsna-withholds-what-you-ask-for|Kṛṣṇa Withholds What You Ask For]], which is the same structure at the level of petition. **There asking is what prevents receiving; here deciding to stop is what produces the thing** — two mechanisms in which the deliberate act defeats itself, and the corpus treats both as features of a relationship rather than as features of minds.

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

**[[ARCHIVES/concepts/psychology/ironic-process-theory|Ironic Process Theory]]** — that page's mechanism is exact and it is this passage's: the act of trying to suppress a thought activates a monitoring process that keeps the thought accessible and primed for return. **Suppression and rebound are not opposites but a single system with two phases**, and the rejection creates the very accessibility the rejection aimed to eliminate. It is not a failure of discipline; it is the architecture.

The pairing is not a comparison — it is the same finding four centuries apart — and what it yields is about how the finding was reached.

**The laboratory route requires a trivial object.** The white bear works as an experiment *because* nobody cares about white bears: the triviality is what isolates the mechanism from any content that might explain the rebound on its own.

**The devotional route requires the opposite.** This passage found the mechanism because the object was the most compelling thing the person could conceive of — and the intensity is what made the sequence noticeable enough to record in the first place.

Which gives the finding neither page reaches. **The two methods have opposite blind spots and they are exactly complementary.** The trivial-object study isolates the mechanism and cannot show anybody why it matters; the maximal-object account shows the stakes with complete clarity and **cannot tell that the mechanism is general**, because with only one object there is no way to see that the object was never the variable.

**And this is why the corpus's attribution is wrong in a way that is not a criticism of it.** *He does not allow Me to forget Him* is precisely the conclusion available from a sample of one — and no amount of care, honesty or observational skill inside that sample would have produced a different answer.

## The Live Edge

**Sharpest implication.** Suppression generates its object twice — once in specifying the instruction and repeatedly in auditing compliance — which is why the appearance follows the resolution instantly rather than eventually. And the two routes to that finding have exactly opposite blind spots: a trivial object isolates the mechanism and hides why it matters, a maximal object shows the stakes and hides that the object was never the variable.

**Generative questions.**
- Four candidate authors for one sentence — Rādhā, Caitanya, Svarūpa Dāmodara, Kṛṣṇadāsa. Is there any way to distribute the credit?
- Every other tradition that noticed this treated it as a problem to defeat. What changes when the mechanism's output is the goal?
- If dropping the audit removes most of the suffering and none of the ground, why does no contemplative tradition in this vault recommend it in those terms?

## Connected Concepts

- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/madana-and-mohana|Mādana and Mohana]] — the taxonomy this is the cleanest instance of
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/condemning-providence|Condemning Providence]] — the same speaker, the opposite tack, the same failure
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/krsna-withholds-what-you-ask-for|Kṛṣṇa Withholds What You Ask For]] — the deliberate act defeating itself, at the level of petition
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/divya-unmada|Divya-unmāda]] — why the failure is filed as an attainment
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/ardha-bahya|Ardha-bāhya]] — the channel, and the authorship problem
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/psychology/ironic-process-theory|Ironic Process Theory]] — the same finding, reached from the trivial end
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/hubs/mental-control-and-suppression-hub|Mental Control & Suppression Hub]] — where the modern literature on this sits
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/hubs/sri-caitanya-hub|Śrī Caitanya Hub]] — the corpus this belongs to

# The Taxonomy That Will Not Sort

## Saguṇa and Nirguṇa, and Then Four More Cuts

Before Śiva gives Satī the nine limbs of bhakti, he gives her the classifications. There are a lot of them, they arrive in about four sentences, and they do not fit together.

> *"O Devī! It is said that **bhakti is of two types, saguṇa and nirguṇa, following the norms and natural.** It is also said to be **superior and inferior.** Based on whether it is **continuous or intermittent**, there are also two differences. Of the two, it is said that **continuous bhakti is of six types.** The learned also know of differences based on **whether it is prescribed, or not prescribed.** **Thus, there are many kinds of bhakti, described elsewhere.** O beloved! As described by sages, **know that there are nine aspects to bhakti.**"*[^1]

Count them. **Saguṇa/nirguṇa. Norm-following/natural. Superior/inferior. Continuous/intermittent — with continuous itself six-fold. Prescribed/not prescribed. And then nine aspects**, on a completely different axis.

Six cuts and a nine-fold list in four sentences, and **not one word about how any of them relate.**

## The Divisions Do Not Compose

Try to build the grid and it collapses immediately.

If bhakti is saguṇa or nirguṇa, **and** superior or inferior, **and** continuous or intermittent, **and** prescribed or not — that is sixteen cells before you add anything. Add the six sub-types of continuous and you have more.

**And none of the nine aspects sits anywhere in that grid.** Hearing, chanting, remembering, tending, serving, worshipping, prostrating, friendly conduct, surrender — these are *activities*. The binaries are *properties*. A person doing śravaṇa could presumably be doing it continuously or intermittently, prescribed or not, in a saguṇa or nirguṇa mode. **The nine cross-cut all of it and the text does not say so.**

Worse, some cuts look like restatements of each other in different vocabulary. *Superior/inferior* against *saguṇa/nirguṇa*: is nirguṇa the superior one? The text does not say. *Norm-following/natural* against *prescribed/not prescribed*: those look like the same distinction twice, and they are given as separate cuts inside the same sentence-run.

## Continuous, of Six Types

The one place the text goes a level deeper is also the one place it stops.

*"Of the two, it is said that continuous bhakti is of six types."*

**Six what?** They are not named. Not one of them. It is the only sub-division in the passage that gets a number and no contents.

That is a specific kind of gap. A list without a number is vague; **a number without a list is a citation** — it points at something the speaker expects to exist elsewhere, in a form he is not reproducing.

And the very next sentence confirms it: *"Thus, there are many kinds of bhakti, **described elsewhere.**"*

## Described Elsewhere

Two words doing an enormous amount of work.

**Śiva, teaching the supreme tattva to Devī, refers her to another text.**

The volume does this rarely. It is a text that prefers to contain things — it gives the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas, the pañca-lakṣaṇa, the thirteen saṃskāras, the eight forms, the five acts, the fifty-seven gaṇa-leaders. When it has a list, it lists.

Here it has at least six classificatory schemes, names none of the six sub-types, and defers.

**The most economical reading is that this passage is a summary of something the compiler had and did not include** — a doxographic paragraph, condensing several existing accounts of bhakti into a run of *"it is said that"* and *"the learned also know of."*

Note the attribution formulas. *It is said. It is also said. The learned also know. As described by sages.* **Four separate hedges in four sentences.** The nine aspects, by contrast, get defined one by one in the speaker's own voice.[^2]

## Analytical Case Study — An Inconsistent Taxonomy Is a Stratigraphy

The build already holds the instrument for this, and this is its cleanest instance.

**A tidy list tells you what its compiler believed. A lumpy one tells you what he inherited and would not discard.** When a list will not sort, stop hunting its principle and count its groups.[^3]

Count the groups here and you get, at minimum:

**A Sāṅkhya-flavoured cut** (saguṇa/nirguṇa).
**A ritual-law cut** (prescribed/not prescribed; norm-following/natural).
**An evaluative cut** (superior/inferior).
**A temporal cut** (continuous/intermittent, six-fold).
**And an activity list** (the nine).

**Those are not one scheme with sub-branches. They are five vocabularies**, from different discourses, laid end to end by someone unwilling to drop any of them.

And the tell is the attribution. The inherited material gets *"it is said"*; the nine get definitions. **The compiler is confident about exactly one of the six schemes**, and it is the one he explains.

## Implementation Workflow

The transferable technique is short and it works on any documentation you did not write.

**When a classification will not compose, stop trying to compose it and read it as sediment.**

Three moves.

**Separate by vocabulary, not by content.** Cuts drawn from different discourses will use different words for the same territory. *Saguṇa/nirguṇa* is metaphysics; *prescribed/not prescribed* is law; *superior/inferior* is evaluation. Three languages means at least three sources.

**Find the one with contents.** In any pile of schemes, one will be worked out and the rest will be named and dropped. **The worked one is the author's; the named ones are inherited.** Here: nine defined, six unnamed, four hedged.

**Then check the hedges.** *It is said. The learned know. Described elsewhere.* Attribution formulas cluster on borrowed material, and they are far more reliable than tone.

The payoff is not pedantic. **A taxonomy you cannot compose is not a bad taxonomy — it is several good ones stacked**, and the practical question changes from *which cell am I in* (unanswerable) to *which scheme is this institution actually running* (answerable, and usually the one with the definitions).

## Count the Groups, Not the Principle

One consequence worth stating plainly, because it applies to this whole volume.

The build has repeatedly found lists in this text that will not resolve: **the eight bonds of Prakṛti defined twice, differently, three hundred endnotes apart.** The **eight forms**, of which the eighth is a *role* rather than a substance, with Debroy noting *"there is thus no unique way to interpret the number eight."* The sages made from body parts, whose taxonomy is *"lumpy"* enough that the build named it a stratigraphy.[^4]

**Four independent cases now, in four different chapters, of a count being load-bearing while its contents are negotiable.**

That is a positive finding about how this text was made rather than a complaint about its rigour. **The number is what was transmitted; the members were re-supplied by whoever was compiling.** Which is exactly what you would expect of material that moved orally in a mnemonic frame and was written down more than once.

## What the Nine Have That the Cuts Do Not

The last observation, and it is the reason the chapter still works.

Everything in the passage is inert except the nine.

The binaries cannot be acted on. Knowing that bhakti is *saguṇa or nirguṇa, superior or inferior, prescribed or not* tells a practitioner nothing about what to do on a given morning. They are **descriptions of a thing already happening.**

The nine are instructions. Each is defined in operational terms — sit steadily and drink in the account; visualise and recite; see him pervading everything; serve at sunrise; offer the sixteen upacāras; do sāṣṭāṅga praṇāma; believe that whatever happens is for your welfare; retain nothing for yourself.[^2]

**And they carry no counts, no ranking, and no cells.**

So the passage runs a classificatory apparatus that cannot be entered and then hands over a practice that can be entered nine ways. **The taxonomy is what the tradition had; the nine are what it could give somebody.** The volume does not distinguish them, and the distinction is the whole value of the chapter.

## Evidence, Tensions, Open Questions

**Strongest support** is the passage at l.1723: six classificatory cuts, a six-fold sub-division with no contents, *"described elsewhere"*, and then the nine aspects on an unrelated axis — all inside four sentences.

**Tension one, and it is the page.** **The cuts do not compose.** Sixteen-plus cells before the six-fold, and **the nine aspects belong to none of them** — activities against properties, with no statement of how they relate.

**Tension two.** Two of the cuts look like **the same distinction in different vocabulary** — *norm-following/natural* and *prescribed/not prescribed* — given as separate divisions in one sentence-run.

**Tension three.** **A number with no contents.** *"Continuous bhakti is of six types"*, and not one is named — followed immediately by *"described elsewhere."* **A number without a list is a citation.**

**Tension four.** The attribution formulas sort the material. *"It is said," "it is also said," "the learned also know," "as described by sages"* — four hedges on the inherited schemes; **the nine get definitions in the speaker's own voice.**

**Open question.** Is the *elsewhere* anywhere? The volume claims five deleted Saṃhitās and admits its own transmission is lossy.[^5] **If no chapter in this Purāṇa names the six types of continuous bhakti, then "described elsewhere" points outside the surviving text**, which is a small but hard datum about what the compiler had in front of him. A single targeted search would settle it.

## Author Tensions & Convergences

[[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/the-nine-limbs-of-bhakti|The Nine Limbs of Bhakti]] is the same passage's other half. **The taxonomy is what the tradition had; the nine are what it could hand somebody** — and the volume does not mark the difference.

[[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/the-eight-bonds-of-prakriti|The Eight Bonds of Prakṛti]] carries two incompatible definitions from two endnotes three hundred apart. **Second case of a count surviving while its contents are re-supplied.**

[[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/the-ashtamurti-eight-forms|The Aṣṭamūrti: Eight Forms]] has an eighth member that is a role rather than a substance, with Debroy conceding *"there is thus no unique way to interpret the number eight."* **Third case.**

[[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/the-sages-made-from-body-parts|The Sages Made From Body Parts]] is where the build first named the instrument — *an inconsistent taxonomy is a stratigraphy.* **This passage is its cleanest specimen: five vocabularies, one worked scheme, four hedges.**

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

**[[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/the-blemishes-taxonomy-failure-modes|The Blemishes Taxonomy: Failure Modes]] (creative-practice).** The Nāṭyaśāstra enumerates what can go wrong in performance — the crown slipping, a mis-struck drum, a stray dog on stage, an actor forgetting a line, cow-dung thrown by a rival company, a meteor. **A named, ordered, teachable *doṣa* taxonomy**, produced by roughly the same culture in roughly the same period as this Purāṇa.

Set them side by side and the difference is not sophistication. **It is who the list had to reach.**

**The Nāṭyaśāstra's taxonomy sorts** because it is a training document for a guild — it has to be transmitted to strangers who will apply it without the author present. Every category has to be distinguishable by someone who was not there.

**The bhakti taxonomy does not sort** because it never had to. It is a doxographic summary, delivered inside a narrative frame, to an interlocutor who already knows the answer.[^6]

What the pair produces: **a taxonomy's internal consistency is a measure of its transmission requirements, not of its author's rigour** — which the build recorded once before and can now state with two cases from one culture.[^3] Which yields a usable inversion: **where you find a lumpy classification, do not conclude the field was confused. Ask who was going to have to use it** — and expect the answer to be *nobody outside the room.*

**[[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/authorship-and-dating-debate|Authorship and Dating Debate]] (history).** You date an undated text by what it mentions. The Arthaśāstra names *china-paṭṭa*, so it postdates 221 BCE; red coral from Alexandria, so it postdates the monsoon trade; *Parasamudra* for Sri Lanka, attested around 100 CE; silver and copper coins but no gold, so before the Guptas. **Pile up the internal evidence and a date emerges. Maybe.**

Chapter 75's classifications are the same evidence type, in a domain where nobody usually looks for it.

**The trade-goods method dates by *objects mentioned*. This dates by *schemes deployed*.** A passage carrying a Sāṅkhya cut, a ritual-law cut, an evaluative cut, a temporal cut and an activity list is carrying five discourses — and discourses, like trade goods, have periods.

The insight neither gives alone: **classification vocabulary is a dateable artefact, and it is more robust than object-mentions because it is harder to interpolate.** A copyist can add a place-name in one word. **Adding a whole classificatory scheme, with its own vocabulary and its own hedging formula, is a much larger intervention** — and it leaves the seam visible, as here, where five schemes sit end to end refusing to compose. Which suggests a method this build has been approaching from the other side: **the layers of a composite text may be readable off its taxonomies more reliably than off its stories**, because a story can be retold smooth and a borrowed classification arrives with its vocabulary attached.

## The Live Edge

**Sharpest implication.** In four sentences before the nine limbs, Śiva gives Satī **six classificatory cuts of bhakti** — saguṇa/nirguṇa, norm-following/natural, superior/inferior, continuous/intermittent, continuous being **six-fold**, and prescribed/not prescribed — **and not one word about how any of them relate.** Build the grid and it is sixteen-plus cells before the six-fold, **and the nine aspects belong to none of them**: activities against properties, cross-cutting everything. Two of the cuts look like the same distinction in different vocabulary. And the six-fold sub-division **has a number and no contents** — *"continuous bhakti is of six types"*, none named — followed immediately by ***"described elsewhere."*** A number without a list is a citation. Read the attributions and the passage sorts itself: *"it is said," "it is also said," "the learned also know," "as described by sages"* — **four hedges on the inherited schemes, while the nine get defined one by one in the speaker's own voice.** Five vocabularies from five discourses, laid end to end by someone unwilling to drop any of them, with exactly one worked out. **The taxonomy is what the tradition had; the nine are what it could hand somebody** — and the volume does not distinguish them.

**Generative questions.**

1. In any pile of schemes, one is worked out and the rest are named and dropped. Is *find the one with contents* the fastest way to identify what an institution actually runs?
2. A taxonomy's consistency measures its transmission requirements, not its author's rigour. **Where you find a lumpy classification, is the right question always *who was going to have to use it*?**
3. Classification vocabulary is harder to interpolate than a place-name. **Are the layers of a composite text more reliably readable off its taxonomies than off its stories?**

## Connected Concepts

- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/the-nine-limbs-of-bhakti|The Nine Limbs of Bhakti]] — the same passage's other half
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/the-eight-bonds-of-prakriti|The Eight Bonds of Prakṛti]] — a count defined twice, differently
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/the-ashtamurti-eight-forms|The Aṣṭamūrti: Eight Forms]] — a count whose contents are negotiable
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/the-sages-made-from-body-parts|The Sages Made From Body Parts]] — where the stratigraphy instrument was named
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/the-three-kinds-of-bhakti|The Three Kinds of Bhakti]] — yet another bhakti classification
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/shravana-kirtana-manana|Śravaṇa, Kīrtana, Manana]] — the three-means framework this does not mention
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/the-five-lost-samhitas|The Five Lost Saṃhitās]] — what "described elsewhere" may be pointing at
